titel: Discounted cash flow step by step
kurz: How a DCF model is worked through in full, and why almost three quarters of the result comes from the terminal value, which can hardly be forecast reliably.

bloecke.md:
A DCF turns assumptions into a single number. The individual steps are simple arithmetic, yet the result looks like a measurement. Only the calculation is precise; the assumptions that go into it remain estimates.

The method needs four building blocks: a cash flow that is freely available after the necessary investments; a period for which this cash flow is planned year by year; an assumption about the time after that; and an interest rate that takes account of risk and time.

bloecke.formel: Value = Σ FCF(t) / (1 + r)^t  +  TV(n) / (1 + r)^n
bloecke.erklaerung: The value is the sum of the present values of all cash flows in the detailed planning period plus the discounted residual value (terminal value) at the end of the planning horizon.
variablen: free cash flow in year t
discount rate: the WACC for FCFF, the cost of equity for FCFE
last year of the detailed planning period
terminal value, the value of all cash flows from year n+1, calculated as at time n

bloecke.md:
## Cash flow and discount rate

There are two internally consistent approaches, which must not be mixed.

**[[Free cash flow to the firm]]** (FCFF) is the cash flow available to all providers of capital, that is, owners and creditors. It is calculated before interest and discounted at the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). The result is the value of the entire operating business, the enterprise value.

**[[Free cash flow to equity]]** (FCFE) is the amount left for the owners after interest, repayments and new borrowing. It is discounted at the cost of equity and leads directly to the value of equity.

The two are linked by an equation: FCFE = FCFF − interest × (1 − tax rate) + net new borrowing. With consistent assumptions, both approaches lead to the same value. German valuation practice under the IDW S1 standard makes the same distinction between the gross approach (entity/WACC), the net approach (flow to equity) and APV.

punkte: EBIT × (1 − s) + depreciation − capital expenditure − increase in working capital
Interest is not included in the cash flow; the tax benefit of interest is reflected in the WACC
The result is the enterprise value; the bridge to equity follows as a separate step
Robust if the capital structure changes during the planning period

rechts.titel: Discounting FCFE at the cost of equity
punkte: Net profit + depreciation − capital expenditure − increase in working capital + net new borrowing
Interest has already been deducted; the tax shield (the tax saving from interest) is included in the cash flow
The result is the equity value directly; no bridge is needed
Standard approach for banks and insurers, where debt is part of the business

bloecke.md: The most expensive mistake in the method is to divide the FCFF discounted at the WACC directly by the number of shares. The result is the value of the entire company, including the part that belongs to the creditors. With €200 million of net debt and 40 million shares, this overstates the value per share by €5; with €1,200 million of net debt, by €30. The same calculation error therefore has a different impact depending on the level of debt.

## Length of the detailed planning period

Five to ten years is usual. A longer period does not make the plan more accurate, because, empirically, company growth is neither easy to predict nor persistent over several years. The horizon should only be long enough for the business to reach a steady state. That includes a constant margin, growth that can be sustained permanently, and investment in fixed assets and working capital that matches this growth. Only from this point may the perpetuity take over. A company that depends on the economic cycle (a cyclical) and is at its earnings peak in year 5 does not meet this condition. The following example simplifies at this point, because the company is still growing at 3% in year 5 and at 1.5% in the perpetuity. A more precise plan would extend the horizon until growth has fallen to the permanent rate.

All figures for this fictitious German industrial supplier are an illustrative calculation. In the base year, revenue is €2,000 million, the EBIT margin 12%, depreciation 5% and capital expenditure 6% of revenue. Working capital tied up amounts to 15% of revenue, and the combined income tax rate is 30%.

The plan assumes revenue growth of 5% in years 1 to 3 and 3% thereafter, with constant margins and ratios. The WACC is 8.5%, the average for mainly German companies in the KPMG Cost of Capital Study 2025. For Industrial Manufacturing, the same study reports 9.4%. Perpetual growth g is 1.5%.

Capital structure: €400 million of net financial debt, €120 million of pension provisions, €30 million of minority interests, €50 million of non-operating assets and 40 million shares.

bloecke.titel: Detailed plan from revenue to present value (€m, illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md:
From year 3 to year 4, FCFF rises from €154.8 million to €166.0 million. That is a larger increase than in any previous year, even though revenue growth falls from 5% to 3% in this year. The working capital line of the table shows why. Growth ties up money in inventories and receivables; slower growth ties up less. The cash outflow for this falls from €16.5 million to €10.4 million, while at the same time capital expenditure rises more slowly.

For every growing company, therefore, growth in the cash flow is first a cost and only later a return. A model in which revenue rises without capital expenditure and working capital growing with it assumes growth without the capital investment it requires.

## Terminal value

The sum of the five present values is €609.4 million. That captures only the smaller part of the value. The terminal value covers everything that happens from year 6 onwards, and measured in present values, that is considerably more.

bloecke.erklaerung: The Gordon growth model calculates the present value of a payment growing at g in perpetuity, as at year 5. Discounted to today (1.085^5 = 1.504), this gives €1,649.3 million.
bloecke.beispiel: Alternatively, the terminal value can be determined using an exit multiple, that is, TV = EBITDA(5) × multiple. Both approaches should be calculated as a cross-check on each other.

bloecke.titel: Present values of the individual years and terminal value
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in € million. The five years of the detailed plan contribute €609.4 million, the terminal value alone €1,649.3 million, which is 73% of the enterprise value.

bloecke.md: The enterprise value is 609.4 + 1,649.3 = €2,258.7 million. Of this, 73% comes from the terminal value and therefore from two inputs, the WACC and g. With plausible variations of these two inputs, the share in this model lies between 68% and 80%. A DCF is therefore less a cash flow forecast than an assumption about the company's end state.

There are two valid objections to this reading, and they make the picture more precise.

First, the share depends on the planning horizon. If you plan ten years individually instead of five, it falls mathematically. The uncertainty remains, however, and shifts to years 6 to 10, which are just as hard to forecast.

Second, in economic terms the “perpetuity” is hardly infinite. Of the €2,480 million terminal value, around €2,010 million comes from years 6 to 30. Only about €470 million, just under a fifth, relates to the period after year 30. The terminal value is therefore above all a statement about the 25 years after the detailed plan.

## Limits for the growth rate g

Three constraints apply to the perpetual growth rate.

1. `g < WACC` must hold. Otherwise the formula is not defined, and the value becomes negative or infinite.
2. `g` must not permanently exceed the long-term nominal growth of the economy, because otherwise the company would mathematically at some point become larger than the entire economy. With an inflation target of 2% and real growth of 0.5% to 1%, any value above about 3% needs its own justification.
3. `g` requires investment. A company that grows at 1.5% forever must also invest in fixed assets and working capital forever. A terminal value with growth but with capital expenditure only equal to depreciation is mathematically inconsistent.

The implied multiple serves as a quick cross-check. The terminal value of €2,480 million corresponds to 5.9 times the EBITDA of year 5 (€417.5 million) and 8.4 times EBIT. If this multiple does not fit the prices paid for comparable companies, something is wrong with the WACC or g. The check also works in the opposite direction. When valuing with an exit multiple, you should back out the growth rate g it contains.

## Bridge to equity value

The enterprise value belongs to all providers of capital. The bridge to the value of equity deducts what is owed to parties other than the shareholders and adds assets that were not included in the operating cash flow.

bloecke.titel: Equity bridge from enterprise value to the value of equity
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in € million. An equity value of €1,758.7 million gives €43.97 per share with 40 million shares.

bloecke.titel: Often underestimated items in the bridge
bloecke.md:
Under Section 253(2) HGB (Commercial Code), pension obligations are discounted at the ten-year average of the market interest rate that matches their remaining term, or optionally at a flat rate for a remaining term of 15 years. Under IAS 19, the yield on high-quality corporate bonds at the reporting date applies. The same obligations therefore often appear at markedly different amounts in the HGB and the IFRS financial statements. The valuer has to decide which figure belongs in the bridge, because it cannot simply be read off.

Share-based payment is non-cash under IFRS 2 and does not appear in FCFF, yet existing shareholders lose part of their stake through this dilution. The diluted share count is therefore what matters.

## Tax rate and tax shield

The 30% in the model is made up of two parts. The first is corporation tax of 15% under Section 23(1) KStG (Corporation Tax Act) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it, together 15.825%. The second is trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), which is calculated as the assessment rate (Steuermesszahl) of 3.5% under Section 11(2) GewStG (Trade Tax Act) multiplied by the municipal multiplier (Hebesatz) under Section 16 GewStG. At the statutory minimum multiplier of 200%, the total burden is around 22.8%; from 2027 the minimum multiplier rises to 280%, and the burden accordingly to around 25.6%. In municipalities with 20,000 or more inhabitants, multipliers in 2025 were between 250% and 580%, which corresponds to around 24.6% to 36.1%. Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich come to 30.2%, 31.9% and 33.0%.

Two German peculiarities reduce the tax shield assumed in the WACC. Section 8 no. 1 GewStG adds a quarter of financing costs back to trade income to the extent that their total exceeds €200,000. For trade tax, interest is therefore only partly deductible. In addition, there is the interest barrier (Zinsschranke) under Section 4h EStG (Income Tax Act) in conjunction with Section 8a KStG. It generally limits the deduction of net interest expense to 30% of tax EBITDA, with an exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of three million euros.

What also matters is the tax actually paid, not the tax reported in the income statement. Declining-balance depreciation for movable assets (Section 7(2) EStG), temporarily reintroduced in 2025, defers tax payments and increases free cash flow in the early years. The immediate tax investment programme (steuerliches Investitionssofortprogramm) adopted in 2025 lays down in law that the corporation tax rate will fall in stages, to 14% in 2028 and then by one percentage point a year to 10% from 2032 (Section 23(1) KStG). A terminal value calculated with today's 30% does not take this reduction into account.

## Sensitivity analysis

A DCF that outputs only a single number is incomplete. A matrix covering the two inputs that most strongly determine the result is more informative.

bloecke.titel: Value per share in euros with varying WACC and g
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. All cash flow assumptions remain unchanged; only the discount rate and perpetual growth are varied. The values range from €34.60 to €64.21.

bloecke.md:
Between the most favourable and the least favourable corner lies a factor of 1.86, and each of the twenty combinations is defensible. One percentage point more WACC lowers the value per share by around 16%; half a percentage point more g raises it by around 8%. No component of the cash flow plan has an effect anywhere near as large.

The method nevertheless remains useful; it is simply used differently. A DCF provides a range and a ranking of the assumptions by their impact. It can also be used to check which corner of this table the current share price already assumes.

With €400 million of net debt at 5%, interest of €20 million is incurred, or €14 million after tax. Without net new borrowing, FCFE in year 1 is therefore 140.4 − 14.0 = €126.4 million. This cash flow is discounted at the cost of equity, not at the WACC.

The matching cost of equity can be derived from the model. Using the calculated equity value of €1,758.7 million and €400 million of net debt as market value weights, around 81% falls on equity. A WACC of 8.5% and a pre-tax cost of debt of 5% then give a cost of equity of around 9.6%. This is close to the KPMG average of 9.7%.

This is where the circularity problem shows. The weights are supposed to be market values, but the market value of equity is the result of the valuation. Ways out are a target capital structure, iterative calculation or the APV approach.

schritte.text: Choose FCFF or FCFE and then stick to that approach throughout.
Adjust for one-off effects, the position in the cycle and capitalised own work before ratios are projected forward.
Make it long enough for a steady state to be plausible, usually five to ten years.
Plan revenue, margin, capital expenditure ratio, working capital ratio and tax rate individually. The cash flow follows from these.
Matching the cash flow, with market value weights and a consistent tax rate.
Gordon growth model with a justified g, then the implied exit multiple as a cross-check.
Deduct net financial debt, pensions and minority interests, add non-operating assets, use the diluted share count.
Calculate the sensitivity to WACC, g and margin, and record in writing which assumption drives the result.

mitnehmen: FCFF is discounted at the WACC and leads to the enterprise value, while FCFE is discounted at the cost of equity and leads directly to the equity value; mixing the two approaches leads to wrong results that can easily go unnoticed.
In the worked model, 73% of the enterprise value comes from the terminal value and therefore depends on the two assumptions WACC and g rather than on the detailed cash flow plan.
One percentage point more WACC lowers the value per share by around 16%, and across plausible ranges of WACC and g the result in the model ranges from €34.60 to €64.21.

Growth costs money at first, because rising revenue ties up working capital and requires investment; a model with growth but without growing capital requirements therefore shows value that is not matched by any capital invested.
For leveraged companies, net debt, pensions, minority interests and dilution in the bridge from enterprise value to equity determine a considerable part of the result.

begriffe.begriff: Free cash flow to the firm
begriffe.text: Cash flow to all providers of capital, calculated before interest as EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + depreciation − capital expenditure − increase in working capital. It is discounted at the WACC and gives the enterprise value.
Cash flow left for the owners after interest, repayments and new borrowing. It is discounted at the cost of equity and gives the value of equity directly.
Present value of all cash flows after the last year of the detailed plan, as at that year. For companies with normal growth, it typically makes up the largest part of the DCF value.

Formula for the terminal value in which the cash flow of the following year is divided by (discount rate minus perpetual growth rate). It assumes constant growth and constant margins from that point on.
Reconciliation from enterprise value to the value of equity. Net financial debt, pension obligations and minority interests are deducted, and non-operating assets are added.

Limit on the tax deduction of net interest expense to, in principle, 30% of tax EBITDA under Section 4h EStG in conjunction with Section 8a KStG, with an exemption threshold of three million euros. It reduces the tax shield in the WACC.
